title: Empanadas
subtitle: latin american baked stuffed pastries
excerpt: Flaky hand-held pastries filled with spiced beef mince. These are baked rather than fried, with a golden egg-washed crust and a filling that stays moist during baking.
sourceNotes: Empanadas are eaten across Latin America, Spain and Portugal. The Argentine and Chilean versions are among the most well-known. This recipe follows the baked Argentine style.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked empanadas on a tray, then transfer to a bag. Bake from frozen at 200C for 30 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch of filling and freeze half for the next round.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the filling up to 2 days ahead. Assemble and bake on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stuffed pastry eaten across Latin America, baked or fried, with fillings ranging from beef to cheese.

content.text: start with a simple shortcrust-style pastry made from flour and cold butter. The filling is a classic picadillo of beef mince with onion, pepper and warm spices. The trick to a good empanada is not overfilling and sealing the edges well so none of the juice escapes during baking.
Chill the pastry before rolling. Warm butter makes it difficult to handle and the edges split when crimped.

items.prepNote: beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash

content.text: Make the filling first. Cook the onion in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 5 minutes. Add the garlic and red pepper and cook for 3 minutes. Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up, for 8 minutes until browned. Add the cumin, paprika, coriander and chilli flakes. Stir well and cook for 2 more minutes. Taste, adjust and leave to cool completely.

Make the pastry. Rub the cold butter into the flour until it resembles breadcrumbs. You can do this in a food processor. Add the egg and ice-cold water and bring together into a smooth dough. Do not overwork. Wrap and chill for 20 minutes.
Preheat the oven to 200C. Roll the pastry on a lightly floured surface to about 4 mm thick. Cut into 15 cm circles using a cutter or a bowl as a guide.
Place 2 tablespoons of cold filling in the centre of each circle. Fold the pastry over to make a half-moon. Press the edges together firmly, then crimp by folding the edge over in small pleats.
Place on a lined baking tray. Brush generously with egg yolk wash. Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until deep golden brown. Leave to cool for 5 minutes before eating.

The filling was too wet or the edges were not sealed well enough. Drain any liquid from the filling before using it. Press the edges firmly and crimp tightly. A fork pressed around the edge adds extra security.

attrs.issue: Pastry is crumbly and hard to roll

content.text: The butter may have been too cold or the dough too dry. Add another tablespoon of cold water and bring together again gently. Over-kneading will toughen it, so handle as little as possible.
Season the filling well before it cools. Cold mince dulls in flavour. Taste while warm and add more cumin and smoked paprika if needed.

Empanadas are eaten from Mexico to Patagonia. Each country has its own version. Argentina bakes them; Colombia fries some and bakes others; Chile adds hard-boiled egg and olive to the filling. In Spain, the empanada is a large pie rather than individual parcels. The word comes from the Spanish empanar, meaning to coat in bread. Every region considers its own version the definitive one.
